content.title: Cocoon Raises $15M To Scale Low-Carbon Cement Alternative
content.text: A large-scale seismic survey is set to begin in Denmark to evaluate subsurface conditions for a proposed carbon capture and storage (CCS) project, marking a key step toward potential onshore CO2 storage development. Smart Seismic Solutions (S3) will deploy more than 50,000 seismic nodes as part of an extensive data acquisition campaign for the Greenstore CCS project. The initiative is located between Randers and Hobro in central Denmark and aims to assess the feasibility of establishing a full-scale CO2 storage site covering roughly 190 square miles. The Greenstore project is operated by Harbour Energy, with partners Ineos Energy and Nordsøfonden. If successful, the project could become operational around 2030. High-resolution data to support storage decisions The seismic campaign is expected to be the largest of its kind conducted onshore in Europe and will play a central role in identifying suitable geological formations for CO2 storage. Data gathered from the survey will inform site selection and support future drilling activities, with the first exploration well planned for 2026, followed by additional wells in 2027. S3 will utilize nodal technology from Stryde, deploying lightweight receivers across approximately 160,000 locations to capture detailed subsurface images. The high-density design is intended to map potential storage formations, including sandstone reservoirs, with greater precision. Relevant: STRYDE Secures Landmark Deal To Supply 42,000 Seismic Nodes For Carbon Capture Project In Denmark The survey will rely on vibroseis trucks to generate controlled ground vibrations, enabling the collection of seismic data while minimizing environmental impact. According to the companies involved, the use of compact, easily deployable nodes allows for more efficient field operations and reduces reliance on heavy equipment. The results of the survey are expected to provide critical insights into Denmark’s geological storage capacity, supporting broader efforts to develop CCS infrastructure in the region. As European countries accelerate decarbonization strategies, projects such as Greenstore are seen as essential to enabling large-scale emissions reductions, particularly for hard-to-abate industrial sectors.
